transcript:
Header:
2026-12-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~60m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Anya (Redwood SE - notes), Priya (Solaris ML), Liam (Infra), Huan (SRE), Carlos (CTO joined at 15:50)

Auto-summary: quick perf deep-dive, agreed profiling matrix, action items on both sides, security docs to be shared.

00:00 Maya: ok yeah thanks all for joining um let's do quick intros then jump into the profiling plan, uh Samir you'll drive the kernel stuff?
00:12 Samir: mm-hmm yeah I'll run through what we typically look at - kernel selection, capture windows for cudagraphs, where TRT-LLM shines and where vLLM scheduling helps.
00:25 Priya: great, we mainly care about p95 latency under 2s for our chat endpoint and throughput for batch offline scoring. sequences vary 512 to 12k tokens, average ~2k.
00:40 Liam: infra constraints: we're on 8xA100 p4d-ish hosts, 600GB GPU memory total per node, private VPC, private registry, strict egress controls.
00:55 Samir: ok good context. quick note - we'll call TensorRT-LLM as TRT-LLM, and vLLM as vLLM, apologies if transcription flips that.
01:05 Anya: also please flag any custom CUDA op in the model; that's a common blocker for TRT conversion.
01:12 Priya: model is a 70B transformer, no custom CUDA ops afaik, some fused ops from our upstream training lib could be present.

02:00 Samir: first, kernel selection: on A100 we see two broad paths - cuBLAS/cuDNN fused kernels (TensorRT) that are highly optimized for static shapes and FP16, and attention kernels (flash-attn) used by vLLM and other runtimes that favor dynamic shapes and batched scheduling. TRT-LLM will pick convolution-y fused matmul kernels, very low per-token latency when you can compile static graphs. vLLM's advantage is scheduling: it aggregates requests into large batches with customized scheduling and KV cache reuse.
02:42 Priya: we care about long contexts; KV cache is critical — what are practical sizes and eviction strategies?
03:00 Samir: KV cache memory scales with sequence length * hidden_size * batch; on 70B that's non-trivial. For long context you want to: 1) pre-allocate big slab to avoid fragmentation, 2) use prefix caching (persist frequently used prefixes), 3) shard KV across GPUs when possible. On TRT-LLM, the static capture approach can reuse KV pointers more efficiently but you may need multiple captured graphs for different prefix lengths. vLLM uses a software-level KV cache that is easier to manage for dynamic lengths but can incur more memory copies.
03:45 Huan: any notes on memory fragmentation? we saw OOMs when switching between short and long sequences.
04:00 Samir: yes fragmentation is common if you alloc/free varying KV sizes. Recommendation: use persistent allocator (jemalloc/cuda malloc pool) and warm-up sequences to prime memory. Also favor contiguous KV layouts for better DMA and NCCL behavior.

06:00 Samir: CUDA Graphs - big win for per-token overhead. Capture the compute graph for the common prefix+step and replay it. Caveats: captures are length/shape sensitive; if your sequence length changes you may need a different graph or use graph patching which is tricky. TRT-LLM captures into TRT engine + cudagraphs gives near-zero CPU overhead. vLLM can leverage cudagraphs too but its dynamic scheduling sometimes conflicts with static captures. Practically we recommend capturing for the most common sequence buckets (e.g., 128, 512, 2048, 8192).
07:05 Priya: and cost of capture? does it add a lot to deploy time?
07:12 Samir: capture time is one-off per engine/shape, could be minutes to tens of minutes depending on warm-up. But maintenance cost if you have many shapes. There's also calibration for INT8 quant which adds another capture/compile step.

09:00 Liam: network & VPC constraints - can Redwood run profiling from our private network? we can't allow egress.
09:15 Maya: yes Redwood Private supports on-prem or VPC-deployed agents; we can run profiling inside your VPC with a transient test runner. We'll share the deployment checklist and KMS flow.
09:30 Samir: for profiling you want local nvprof/NSYS traces and cupti counters; we usually ask the customer to run NVTX annotated runs and upload traces to an S3 bucket or share via secure link. If registry is private we can pull images via auth token.

11:00 Samir: TRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs - summary: TRT-LLM: best for latency P50/P95 when you can compile with static-ish shapes and use FP16/INT8; less flexible for extremely dynamic mixed-batch sizes. vLLM: excellent throughput via software scheduling, dynamic batching, and KV reuse; easier to support many sequence lengths without many engine builds. For Solaris long-context chat use-case, TRT-LLM + multiple captured graphs + smart routing to variant models might hit your p95 targets if you invest operationally. If you need quick deploy and lots of dynamic lengths, vLLM will be faster to get started.
11:55 Priya: what about quantization? we've been looking at Q4 and INT8. stability concerns for LLMs.
12:10 Samir: q4 (LLM.int8 or GPTQ-like) can work with careful calibration and validation suite. TRT-LLM has INT8 engines but requires representative calibration data; post-training quantization sometimes loses sample-level quality. vLLM has plugins for experimental quant kernels but performance vs accuracy varies. We recommended a small eval harness with BLEU/LLM-based metrics and real prompts to validate quality.
12:50 Anya: note: for evaluation we look at both prompt-level divergence and downstream metric like hallucination rate.

14:00 Priya: any ops tips for kernel selection? e.g., when does TRT pick different kernels?
14:15 Samir: TRT kernel selection depends on shapes, compute capability, and whether the layer fits the fused pattern. It will choose different GEMM strides and algorithms; sometimes it falls back to cuBLAS if a fused kernel isn't available. Important to inspect TRT logs and kernel timing; TRT Inspector and Nsight can show which kernels dominate. Also watch for type mismatches (FP16->FP32 fallbacks) which kill perf.
14:50 Huan: we've seen variances in p95 across identical runs - jitter. any debugging tips?
15:00 Samir: jitter often from OS-level interrupts, PCIe traffic, or BG cuda graphs get recompiled; ensure GPU frequency governor is locked, isolate NIC interrupts, pin processes to cores. Also check CUDA kernel launches for occasional syncs - missing stream usage can serialize.

17:00 Maya: quick discussion on routing & fallbacks - Redwood can route requests by policy. If a TRT engine for 8k is busy, requests can fall back to vLLM instance (higher latency but still up). That's part of our graceful degradation story.
17:30 Liam: good - that's desired. how complex is the rollout to have both runtimes?
17:40 Samir: it's operationally heavier but doable; you need consistent model weights, tokenizer and evaluation to ensure parity. We recommend small canary sets to validate outputs between runtimes.

20:00 Priya: final: what data do you need from us to run the profiling?
20:10 Samir: model weights, representative prompt set, target latency/throughput SLOs (you gave p95=2s), and VPC infra details. Also confirm if INT8 is allowed.
20:25 Priya: yes INT8 ok for some features, not for safety-critical responses. we'll mark those.

22:00 Carlos (CTO - joined): thanks all, make sure security checklist is reviewed. If TRT-LLM path looks promising, we'll commit to pilot.

Recap & close: agreed profiling matrix (8k/16k shapes; 128/512/2048 buckets), TRT-LLM and vLLM runs, cudagraphs capture for top buckets, calibration for INT8, and follow-ups.

Artifacts referenced: perf spreadsheet (link placeholder: https://redwood.ai/sheets/solaris-perf), NVTX/NSYS trace samples, TRT engine logs, Redwood Private VPC checklist (link placeholder).

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and misheard acronyms (T-R-T transcribed as "tea-are-tee"), some words may be garbled.
